## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Kapijātaka* (Ja 404), titled *The Monkey* in modern translation, is a narrative preserved in the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. The story opens with an introductory tale set at Jetavana near Sāvatthī, framed around the event of Devadatta being swallowed up by the earth [SuttaCentral]. Hearing the monks in the Hall of Truth discussing the fate of Devadatta and his community, the Buddha explains that Devadatta had previously brought about the ruin of himself and his company, prompting the telling of this past-life narrative [SuttaCentral].
In the conclusion (*samodhāna*) of the tale preserved in the commentary, the Buddha identifies the characters of the past: the disobedient, refractory monkey (*dubbacakapi*) was Devadatta, his monkey retinue represented Devadatta's partisan followers, and the wise monkey king (*paṇḍitakapi rājā*) who modeled appropriate discipline was the Bodhisatta himself [Fausböll 1883].
DharmaNexus identifies extensive textual reuse within Pali literature between this text and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (third volume), with four matching segments (742 shared characters; longest match §0.4–7.4 corresponding to §3228_9–3249 at 0.95 similarity) [DharmaNexus]. DharmaNexus also records machine alignments with a Tibetan text, the *Pravacanaratnākhyānaśākyavaṃśāvalī* (D4357), registering nine shared passages (best score 25; §2.3–2.4 aligning with §305a-24) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations of the jātaka across four languages [SuttaCentral].
